catalog_locator: p. 350, sec. 6 Conclusion, Table 6 'Comparative features of Baka-Gundi languages' (Limassa column) with fn. 5; background p. 343, sec. 2.2 Tone.
catalog_quote: p. 343, sec. 2.2 Tone: "Like all known Mundu-Baka members, Ngundi is a tone language. It features three lexical register tones, namely high (H), mid (M), and low (L). High tone is marked by ´, low tone by `, whilst mid tone is diacritically unmarked. ... Contour tones occur only on long vowels or diphthongs, suggesting the mora as the tone-bearing unit. VV-sequences and thus contour tones are scarce." p. 350, sec. 6 Conclusion: "This sketch proves Ngundi’s close relationship to Limassa and Baka+. In Table 6, I provide an overview of the discussed features in comparison. Feature | Baka+ 4 | Ngundi | Limassa 5 / Vowel system | 7 vowels | 7 vowels | 7 vowels / ... / Tone levels | 3 tone levels | 3 tone levels | 3 tone levels / Syllable structure | only open syllables, identical types ... Table 6 Comparative features of Baka-Gundi languages" fn. 5: "The data on Limassa were generated in the course of my ongoing Ph.D. project."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (11 pp, text; the PDF's metadata gives the title 'A comparative sketch of Ngundi', author Benedikt Winkhart; edoc HU doi:10.18452/32606, open access) and its. At the stated locators the quoted passages are present: p.350 sec. 6 Conclusion reads 'This sketch proves Ngundi's close relationship to Limassa and Baka+. In Table 6, I provide an overview of the discussed features in comparison.' followed by Table 6 with columns Baka+ [fn4] / Ngundi / Limassa [fn5] and rows 'Vowel system: 7 vowels / 7 vowels / 7 vowels', 'Tone levels: 3 tone levels / 3 tone levels / 3 tone levels', 'Syllable structure: only open syllables, identical types', and footnote 5 'The data on Limassa were generated i…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Limassa is a three-level register-tone language (H, M, L) with only open syllables, per the fieldworker's own PhD data; the source says nothing about word stress or accent in Limassa (or in Ngundi).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the Limassa information is a comparative table cell, not a prosodic description.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns lexical tone inventory only; no word- or phrase-level stress/accent claim exists in any opened source. The chapter describes Ngundi; Limassa figures as comparandum from Winkhart's unpublished Limassa documentation (ELDP 2016-2020, Bomassa, Rep. of Congo).
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand data come from Winkhart's ELDP fieldwork in Bomassa (and Boncoin, Kabo) on the Sangha River, northern Republic of Congo (ELAR: 40-45 speakers), not the Central African Republic location Glottolog gives; same language, lima1246 / ISO bme (Bomassa/Bamassa). The quoted source is a sketch of the sister language Ngundi (ngun1272? Glottolog 'Gundi' gdi) in which Limassa appears as a comparandum; the Limassa cells are explicitly the author's own PhD field data.

sources.citation: Winkhart, Benedikt. 2015. The Reconstruction of Baka-Mundu (Ubangi, Niger-Congo): On the Historical Comparison of the Nominal System. Handout, HU Berlin Linguistic Colloquium, 7 July 2015, 23 pp. (MA project; Internet Archive copy of HU site PDF).
sources.note: Family-level typological note only (p.4): 'All languages are tone languages with three tones (high, mid, and low).. Every syllable constitutes a tone baring unit. Tone is both lexical and grammatical.' No stress statement; Limassa data there are second-hand (Ouzilleau 1911 list VIII, Bruel 1910-11, Klieman 1997 wordlists).
